validated_issues.original_description: Uses 'system' with 'rm -rf' for cleanup. While safe here with hardcoded paths, it's less portable than using Scheme-native file deletion if available.
validated_issues.reasoning: CONFIRMED but line number was slightly off (report said 148, actual is 142 and 506). The use of (system "rm -rf ...") with a hardcoded test path (.test-graph-algorithms) is safe in this context but not portable across all platforms. This is a reasonable low-severity style/portability concern for a test file.

validated_issues.original_description: map-collection throws an error if a block is missing, while fold-collection and filter-collection silently skip them. This inconsistency could lead to unexpected crashes in distributed environments.
validated_issues.reasoning: CONFIRMED. map-collection (line 69) explicitly calls (error ...) when a block is not found, while fold-collection (line 92) and filter-collection (line 77-81) silently skip missing blocks. This API inconsistency violates the principle of least surprise and could cause unexpected crashes when migrating code between these functions.

validated_issues.original_description: collection-group-by has O(N^2) complexity due to nested map/assoc usage for each element. For large collections, this will be significantly slow.
validated_issues.reasoning: CONFIRMED. The implementation at lines 184-203 uses assoc (O(K) where K=groups) plus map over all groups (O(K)) for each element, resulting in O(N*K) which degrades to O(N^2) when each element has a unique key. However, for typical use cases with few groups, performance is acceptable. Low severity is appropriate.

validated_issues.original_description: collection-add and collection-merge do not check for duplicate hashes, which might lead to unexpected growth if called repeatedly with the same members.
validated_issues.reasoning: CONFIRMED. collection-add (line 220-226) prepends without deduplication, and collection-merge (lines 243-250) even documents '(may have duplicates)' in its comment. This is intentional behavior per the comment but could cause unexpected storage growth. Low severity is appropriate as it's documented behavior.

validated_issues.original_description: (cdr (assq 'body post)) will crash if a post is missing the 'body' field (assq returns #f). This occurs in multiple functions: find-tagged, list-all-tags, tag-histogram, etc.
validated_issues.reasoning: CONFIRMED. HIGH severity is correct. At line 41, (cdr (assq 'body post)) will throw an error if 'body is missing because assq returns #f and (cdr #f) is invalid. This pattern appears at lines 41, 71, 94, 136, and 148. The file header claims to be 'Shell-tier code' with 'defensive patterns' but these defensive patterns are missing for this critical case. Any malformed post without a 'body' field will crash the query system.

validated_issues.original_description: count-occurrences is O(N^2) because it calls remove-assq inside a loop over the input list. Scalability issue for high tag counts.
validated_issues.reasoning: CONFIRMED. The count-occurrences function (lines 103-114) calls remove-assq (which uses filter - O(K)) inside the main loop over N symbols, giving O(N*K) complexity. When K approaches N (many unique tags), this becomes O(N^2). Medium severity is appropriate - this will become a bottleneck with large forums but is acceptable for small datasets.

validated_issues.original_description: Functions like find-tagged and tag-histogram call collect-all-posts on every invocation. In a large forum, this causes massive I/O overhead without caching.
validated_issues.reasoning: CONFIRMED. collect-all-posts (lines 55-59) iterates all channels and loads all posts. Functions find-tagged (line 38), list-all-tags (line 68), tag-histogram (line 91), tag-values (line 133), and tag-value-histogram (line 147) all call collect-all-posts without any caching mechanism. For a forum with many posts, this causes repeated I/O operations. Medium severity is appropriate - this is a scalability concern but not a correctness bug.

gaps_found.description: collection-all? has inconsistent missing-block behavior: it returns #f immediately when encountering a missing block (treating it as predicate failure), while collection-any? via collection-find would skip missing blocks. This creates asymmetric semantics between the two functions.

foldr-collection note in docstring says 'Function signature is (Block A -> A) to match foldr convention' but this is actually reversed from how fold-collection works (A Block -> A). While documented, this inconsistency between fold-collection and foldr-collection function signatures may cause user confusion.

count-string-occurrences (lines 159-170) has the same O(N^2) complexity issue as count-occurrences - it calls remove-assoc inside the loop. QA only mentioned count-occurrences but missed this duplicate pattern.

Convenience functions find-by-tag, tags, and tag-report (lines 241-252) assume (fs) procedure is defined in scope. If called before REPL initialization, these will fail with an undefined variable error. Should have a guard or clearer documentation.

summary.notes: All 7 issues from the original QA report were confirmed valid with accurate severity ratings. The high-severity issue in query.ss (missing defensive checks for assq returning #f) is the most critical finding. The QA agent did good work but missed 4 additional issues: an inconsistency in collection-all? behavior, a confusing function signature inconsistency in foldr-collection, a duplicate O(N^2) pattern in count-string-occurrences, and unguarded convenience functions in query.ss. Overall, the flashmob QA was thorough and accurate - 100% confirmation rate with reasonable severity assessments.
